text: On market day peasants and their wives. <break time="0.8s" /> Were walking along every road. <break time="0.8s" /> Toward the little town of Goderville. <break time="0.8s" /> Bent by years of hard work in the fields. <break time="0.8s" /> The men moved slowly. <break time="0.8s" /> With long, heavy steps. <break time="0.8s" /> The women carried baskets. <break time="0.8s" /> Full of chickens and ducks. <break time="0.8s" /> Hurrying to the square. <break time="0.8s" /> Where the market was held. <break time="0.8s" /> Among them was Maître Hauchecorne of Bréauté. <break time="0.8s" /> Who had just arrived. <break time="0.8s" /> At the edge of the town. <break time="0.8s" /> Walking toward the square. <break time="0.8s" /> He noticed a little piece of string. <break time="0.8s" /> Lying on the ground. <break time="0.8s" /> Like every true Norman. <break time="0.8s" /> He believed that anything useful should be picked up. <break time="0.8s" /> So he bent down slowly. <break time="0.8s" /> His old back hurt. <break time="0.8s" /> From rheumatism. <break time="0.8s" /> But he took the string from the ground. <break time="0.8s" /> And began to roll it up carefully. <break time="0.8s" /> Just then. <break time="0.8s" /> He saw Maître Malandain. <break time="0.8s" /> The harness maker. <break time="0.8s" /> Watching him. <break time="0.8s" /> From the doorway of his shop. <break time="0.8s" /> The two men had once quarreled. <break time="0.8s" /> About a halter. <break time="0.8s" /> And they had never forgiven each other. <break time="0.8s" /> Since that day. <break time="0.8s" /> Feeling ashamed. <break time="0.8s" /> To be seen picking up string. <break time="0.8s" /> Hauchecorne quickly hid it. <break time="0.8s" /> In his pocket. <break time="0.8s" /> And pretended to search the ground.
